newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African doctors apologise to Biko family.
newsitem.headline: S.African doctors apologise to Biko family.

text.p: Two South African doctors made a public apology on Tuesday to the family of black activist Steve Biko, who died after repeated police torture which state physicians failed to try to stop.

The apologies were issued at a special hearing of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, which was called to probe the role of the medical profession during the apartheid years.

Peter Folb, professor of pharmacology at the University of Cape Town, read out an English translation of a haiku -- a form of short Japanese poetry -- which he said he had written in Xhosa to honour Biko's memory.
"A sombre duty, describing the country's loss, before his loved ones," the poem read.
"I wish to address some personal words to the family of Steve Biko... To extend to them as far as I am able, and on behalf of every doctor who feels this way, an apology," Folb said.
Biko's widow Ntsika and brother Khaya attended the hearing. Ntsika Biko has previously objected to the commission's mandate to grant amnesty to the policemen who killed her husband.

"I wish to give you an undertaking that those ethical and human issues neglected in the case of Steve Biko will be remembered and continue to be addressed and corrected to the best of our abilities," Folb said.

Biko died in 1977 after weeks of interrogation by security police, who on several occasions allowed the black consciousness leader to be examined by two state physicians. The doctors failed to order a halt to assaults on the detainee, saying afterwards they did not think they had the power to do so.
"There was abject acceptance by individual doctors, and by their organised profession, of interference by the state and by the police in the conduct of their professional activities," Folb said.
Folb noted that Biko's was only one of dozens of similar cases.
Wendy Orr, a member of the truth commission and herself a medical doctor, said she wanted to be associated with Folb's apology.
"If we achieve anything through this process, I hope that we ensure that human beings are never again treated like animals, the way Steven Biko was," she said.

The commission received a report compiled by doctors at the University of Cape Town and therapists working with victims of torture which said doctors, nurses and others had committed widespread abuses during the apartheid years.
"These abuses arose in a context in which the entire fabric of the health sector was permeated by apartheid and in which human rights were profoundly devalued," the report said.
It cited the example of an army psychiatrist who had used aversion therapy to try to change the sexual orientation of homosexual conscripts.

It said the doctor showed the conscripts pictures of men and invited them to fantasise about them, then gave the conscripts electric shocks. When the shocks stopped, the doctor immediately showed his patients pictures of naked women.
